title: Interpreting Federal Reserve Announcements and Interest Rate Decisions
content:
The Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) holds eight scheduled policy meetings each year. These meetings represent some of the most market-moving events on the global economic calendar, setting the Federal Funds Rate that anchors borrowing costs worldwide.

The Federal Funds Rate is the interest rate at which commercial banks lend reserve balances to other banks overnight. Adjustments to this benchmark rate trigger ripple effects throughout the economy, directly influencing rates for mortgages, auto loans, credit cards, and corporate borrowing.

During FOMC announcements, markets parse three elements: the official policy rate decision, the Summary of Economic Projections (often called the 'Dot Plot'), and Fed Chair Jerome Powell's post-meeting press conference. The Dot Plot shows where each FOMC member expects interest rates, inflation, and GDP to sit over the next several years, offering a window into the central bank's policy trajectory.

When reading Fed news, notice terms like 'Hawkish' and 'Dovish.' A hawkish Fed emphasizes fighting inflation by raising interest rates or keeping them higher for longer, which can slow economic growth and compress stock valuations. A dovish Fed prioritizes boosting employment by cutting interest rates or expanding liquidity, which tends to stimulate asset prices. Long-term investors should follow Fed policy to understand borrowing costs, without attempting to day-trade interest rate headlines.
